newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian PM defends govt metalworkers' proposal.
newsitem.headline: Italian PM defends govt metalworkers' proposal.

text.p: Government proposals drawn up to try to end the long-running pay dispute in the metalworkers and engineering sector were fair and would not fuel inflation, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Tuesday.
The employers' federation, Federmeccanica, have rejected the government suggestions as "unacceptable".

Talks between unions and management to resolve the six-month old row broke down last week. In a bid to break the impasse, the government suggested that workers should be given a 200,000 lire ($130) a month pay rise for the 1996-1998 contract period.
"This is a very fair offer which doesn't favour either side," Prodi told reporters.
The government proposals have been welcomed by trade unions, who had been asking for 230,000 lire a month for their 1.7 million members.

But Federmeccanica, which had offered a pay rise of 139,000 lire, said on Monday that if they accepted the suggested deal it would mean an average wage increase of 10.3 percent over the two year period compared to government forecasts of an inflation rate of less than 4.5 percent.
Prodi said it would be less costly.
"(The government) proposal foresees a 6.1 percent increase. In real terms this means a 1.5 percent increase over two years -- 0.75 percent a year," Prodi said.

Union leaders on Tuesday blasted the employers' rejection of the government intervention, warning of possible industrial action. "It will be a hot January. We have not discarded our strike weapon," Sergio Cofferati, leader of Italy's largest trades' union federation, the Cigl, told La Repubblica daily.
Labour Minister Tiziano Treu told the same newspaper he hoped to call unions and management back to the negotiating table on January 2 or 3. ($1 = 1,525)
